newsitem.title: UK: Ozone agreements can cut cancer risk - researchers.
newsitem.headline: Ozone agreements can cut cancer risk - researchers.

text.p: Cases of skin cancer will quadruple by the year 2100 if ozone-depleting chemicals are not restricted, scientists reported on Wednesday.

But the strictest versions of current agreements, if implemented, will cut the increase to just 10 percent by 2050, the researchers at the Netherlands' Institute of Public Health and the Environment said.
"It is very important to follow these agreements. It means a tremendous reduction in ozone-related risks," Harry Slaper, who led the research, said in a telephone interview.
Slaper's group based the findings on a complex analysis of current cases, skin cancer tests on mice and projections of ozone levels.

A 1985 agreement known as the Vienna Convention set up a framework for reducing production of chemicals that harm the ozone layer. These chemicals include chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), used widely in refrigeration and aerosols.
The latest set of agreements, known as the Copenhagen Amendments, were signed in 1992 and called for production of five of the worst offenders to stop at the end of 1995.
However, there is still a significant black market in the chemicals.
Slaper's group looked at what would happen had there been no agreement and also examined figures for the interim 1987 Montreal Protocol and the stricter Copenhagen Amendments.

"We evaluated the skin cancer types: squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, the most frequent but least aggressive, and cutaneous malignant melanoma, the least frequent but most aggressive," they wrote in the science journal Nature.
Skin cancer cases due to ozone depletion would double in the United States under the Montreal agreement, they found. But they would have more than quadrupled had there been no agreement.

They would grow 10 percent by 2050 if all production of ozone-depleting chemicals had actually stopped, as agreed at the end of 1995, and then fall to two percent by 2100. Figures were just slightly lower for northwest Europe.

Slaper said he had not taken into account problems implementing the agreements. "Although they are probably not fully met, we do not enter into that debate," he said. "We just make an observation of what would happen if the schedule is fully implemented to the sharpest protocol."
He said even the imperfect reductions that had been made had started to do some good. "There are already more than strong indications that there was a large reduction achieved," he said.
"To fully implement the Copenhagen amendment, if that is achieved, we can reduce future skin cancer risks due to ozone depletion tremendously."
A second report in Nature found that the ozone hole over Antarctica would start to "heal" by early next century, provided agreements are honoured.

David Hofmann of the U.S. weather service NOAA said the first signs would been seen by 2008. "The ozone layer would then continue to heal slowly, reaching pre-ozone hole levels by about the year 2050," he wrote.
